title: Enterprise Dedicated — SLA negotiation primer and transient-burst policy for heterogeneous GPU fleets
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description: This ticket captures a canonical negotiation primer and a recommended transient-burst policy aimed at enterprise customers requesting Dedicated GPU capacity. It covers: SLA target bands (p50/p95 latency, throughput guarantees), reservation vs. burst semantics, GPU-class mapping (A100/RTX/Infer/T4 equivalents), preemption and priority rules, cost allocation options for burst consumption, routing/fallback strategies to hosted or lower-tier pools, telemetry needed to validate SLOs, and ops runbooks for exceptional events. The deliverable will be a one-page negotiation checklist + a technical appendix for engineering that specifies autoscaling knobs, backfill/preemption behaviour, and required metrics/events for alerts.
acceptance_criteria: A concise negotiation checklist (1 page) exists and is validated with Sales/CS/Infra
Technical appendix that maps workload patterns to GPU family recommendations and autoscale bounds
Clear definition and implementation plan for 'burst credits' including billing implications
Fallback policy defined: when and how traffic automatically routes to compatible hosted models or downgraded GPU classes
Ops runbook for SLA degradations including thresholds, recovery steps, and customer communication templates
decisions: Adopt tiered SLA bands: Bronze (best-effort), Silver (p95 latency target), Gold (p95 + reserved throughput guarantee)
Support transient bursts up to a configurable 'burst credit' pool per customer; bursts billed at a premium rate and capped by policy
Map GPU families to recommended workload archetypes (large-context serving -> A100/HH-family; high-throughput embeddings/rerank -> T4/Infer equivalents)
Use prioritized preemption (low-priority worker shards are evicted first) with at-least-one fallback region for Gold customers
tradeoffs: Strict reserved-throughput guarantees reduce utilization and increase cost for customers; offering burst credits improves utilization but complicates billing
Aggressive preemption lowers cost but increases risk of customer-visible latency spikes during peak reclaim events
Routing to hosted model variants preserves availability but may expose customers to model/version differences requiring explicit acceptance
